solution: The verb 'understand' is stative: it names a mental state rather than an action unfolding in time, and verbs of that class are not used in the continuous tenses. One may write 'she understood his point of view' or 'she had understood his point of view', but not 'she was understanding his point of view'. The form 'was understanding' is acceptable only in the quite different case where 'understanding' is an adjective meaning sympathetic or tolerant, as in 'she was very understanding'. That reading is closed off here because the word is followed by the direct object 'his point of view', which can only be the object of a verb, so the progressive form stands and is wrong. The rest of the sentence is sound: the backshift of tense in reported speech is correctly handled, 'his point of view' is a normal noun phrase, and 'very well' modifies the verb properly. The fault therefore lies in the opening segment. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: \(\underline{\text{Which}}\) way shall we go?
solution: The word 'which' belongs to a small group of question words that can work in two different ways. Standing on its own in place of a noun, as in 'Which is your bag?', it is an interrogative pronoun. Attached to a noun, as it is here, it tells us which particular 'way' is meant, and so it does the work of a qualifying word describing a noun; in that use it is called an interrogative adjective. Since it modifies the noun 'way' rather than replacing it, the second use is the one in this sentence. Testing the other labels confirms it: the word names no person, place or thing, so it is not a noun; it is not a verb form ending in -ing pressed into service as a noun, so it is not a gerund; and it links no two clauses together, so it is not a conjunction. Matches option D.

Therefore, “owing” is a preposition in this sentence.

stem: Flow velocities in an incompressible fluid can be measured with which one of the following?
solution: A Venturi tube is an instrument used to determine the flow velocity of incompressible fluids based on Bernoulli’s principle. The tube has a narrowed section where fluid velocity increases, leading to a corresponding drop in pressure. By comparing the pressure difference between two points, the flow velocity can be derived.

stem: The following questions consist of two statements, one labelled as the Assertion (A) and the other as the Reason (R). You are to examine these two statements carefully and select the answers to these items using the codes given below: Assertion (A): If a barometer carries water instead of mercury, the height of the column corresponding to a pressure equivalent to 76 cm of mercury increases. Reason (R): The specific heat of water is greater than that of mercury.
optA: Both A and R are individually true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
optB: Both A and R are individually true, and R is the NOT correct explanation of A.
optC: A is true, but R is false.
optD: A is false, but R is true.
solution: Take the two statements separately. A barometer works by balancing the pressure of the atmosphere against the pressure at the foot of a liquid column, so \(P = h\rho g\) with the same \(P\) whichever liquid is used. Mercury has a relative density of about 13.6 and water of 1, so equating the two columns gives \(h_{w}\rho_{w} = h_{m}\rho_{m}\), that is \(h_{w} = 76 \times 13.6\) centimetres, roughly 1034 cm or about 10.3 metres. The column is therefore very much taller with water than with mercury, and the assertion is true. The reason is also true taken by itself: the specific heat capacity of water is about 4200 joules per kilogram per kelvin against roughly 140 for mercury, one of the largest such differences among common liquids. But specific heat measures how much energy is required to raise a substance's temperature, and no heating takes place in a barometer at all. The property that fixes the height of the column is the density of the liquid, not its specific heat. Both statements are true, then, but the second does not explain the first. Matches option B.

The reason is separately true as a fact of physics (water about 4200 J/kg/K, mercury about 140), but specific heat governs how much energy warms a substance and nothing in a barometer is heated; the governing property is density. stem: A heavy ball is suspended as shown in the figure given above. A quick jerk on the lower string will break that string but a slow pull on the lower string will break the upper string. The first result occurs because: Upper string Lower string
optA: the force is too small to move the ball.
optB: air friction holds the ball back.
solution: Inertia is the property of an object that causes it to resist any change in its state of motion. When a sudden jerk is applied to the lower string, the force is applied abruptly. Due to inertia, the ball resists this rapid change in motion, causing the lower string, which is weaker, to break. Conversely, when the force is applied slowly, the ball has time to gradually adjust to the increasing force. As a result, the tension in the upper string becomes greater than in the lower string, ultimately causing the upper string to break.

subject: Physics
stem: One feels heavier in a lift when the lift
solution: A person feels heavier in a lift when it just begins to go up. This is because the body gains inertia from being at rest and pushes against gravity. Here are some other things to know about feeling heavier in a lift: Accelerating upwards: When a lift accelerates upwards, the apparent weight of the person inside it increases. Reaching a constant speed: When the elevator reaches a constant speed, the person feels normal again. Stopping: When the elevator stops, the person feels heavier for an instant.

solution: A spherical air bubble embedded in a piece of glass behaves like a diverging lens when a ray of light passes through it. subject: Physics
stem: Two metallic wires A and B are of same material and have equal length. If the cross-sectional area of B is double that of A, which one among the following is the electrical resistance of B?
solution: The resistance of a wire is directly proportional to its length (L) and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area (A). This relationship is given by: R = rL/A Where * R is the resistance. * r is the resistivity of the material. * L is the length. * A is the cross-sectional area. In this case, both wires A and B are made of the same material, so their resistivity (r) is the same. They also have the same length (L). If the cross-sectional area of B is double that of A (A–B = 2A–A), then the resistance of B will be half that of A. Therefore, the correct answer is (d) 1/2 that of A.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which one of the following is not a mixture?
solution: Mercury is not a mixture. It is a pure substance and a chemical element, represented by the symbol Hg on the periodic table. It’s also known as quicksilver. Air consists of a mixture of gases, mainly nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide, and small amounts of other gases. Milk is an emulsion, which is a combination of fat droplets dispersed in water, along with dissolved proteins, sugars, and minerals. Cement is a mixture of different compounds, including limestone, clay, gypsum, and other materials that are finely ground together.

stem: Dry ice is used for making cold-baths in laboratories by mixing it with volatile organic solvents. Identify the form of dry ice from the following.
solution: Dry ice is the solid state of carbon dioxide (CO2), which sublimates directly from solid to gas at room temperature. This property makes it an ideal cooling agent, as it does not leave any liquid residue. Due to its extremely low temperature of −78.5°C (−109.3°F), dry ice is widely used in laboratories and various cooling applications.

stem: An oxidising agent is a substance which:
optA: increases the oxidation number of an element in a given substance.
optB: decreases the oxidation number of an element in a given substance.

solution: Capillarity (or capillary action) refers to the ability of a liquid to flow in narrow spaces without the assistance of external forces (like gravity). This phenomenon is crucial in several everyday processes. If capillarity didn’t exist, the following would be affected: Kerosene lamp: In a kerosene lamp, capillary action draws the liquid kerosene up into the wick. Without capillarity, the fuel wouldn’t rise to the wick, and the lamp wouldn’t work. Using a straw: Drinking through a straw relies on capillary action and the creation of a pressure difference. Without capillarity, one wouldn’t be able to draw the liquid up the straw. Blotting paper: Blotting paper works by capillary action, which absorbs liquids. Without capillarity, the paper would fail to absorb and hold liquids. Plants: Plants rely on capillary action to draw water from the roots up through the stem and into the leaves. Without capillarity, plants wouldn’t be able to transport water and nutrients, making life on Earth unsustainable for them. Thus, all four statements are correct as they all depend on capillary action.

solution: The question asks which description is not correct, so three of the four should match the standard definitions and one should not. Cross-breeding is correctly described: superior males of one breed are mated with superior females of a different breed. Out-crossing is correctly described as well, in that the offspring produced by such a mating is itself termed an out-cross. Out-breeding is the general name for the mating of unrelated animals, and the account given, animals of the same breed carrying no common ancestor over the preceding four to six generations, is a recognised description of it. In-breeding, however, is defined as the mating of more closely related animals within the same breed over four to six generations, not over one or two. The number matters, because the purpose of in-breeding is to raise homozygosity and expose the recessive traits that selection can then act on, and a single generation or two of it would achieve nothing of the kind. The period stated in that description is therefore wrong. Matches option A.

solution: The normal lapse rate is the average fall in air temperature with increasing height through the troposphere.
